extracted.intended_audience: military legal officers, paymasters, and administrators handling pay/allowances and court-martial consequences
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of legal rules and standards governing military pay, allowances, forfeitures, stoppages, and related entitlements (clothing, commutation, travel) including interaction with courts-martial and administrative orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations may authorize gratuitous issues or increased allowance for campaign-destroyed clothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations providing for gratuitous issues or an increase of the clothing allowance to replace articles practically destroyed in carrying on a campaign are legally permissible and may be made retroactive to cover issues already made under such conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Department commander directed gratuitous issue of khaki uniform items after Manila attack (Aug. 13, 1898); opinion C.6862, Feb. 1899 holds such regulation valid and retroactive when replacing articles destroyed under extraordinary campaign conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gratuitous issue for clothing destroyed to prevent contagion
rubrics_metrics.description: Where clothing of enlisted men has been destroyed to prevent contagion, a gratuitous issue of such clothing will be made to the enlisted men upon the certificate of an officer with personal knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circular 57, A.G.O., 1898; held there is no provision for paying for the clothing destroyed in lieu of the gratuitous issue (C.5588, Jan. 1899; 20143, Aug. 1906).

rubrics_metrics.name: No clothing-account credit for clothing lost by fire/casualty
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier is not entitled to be credited in his clothing account with the value of clothing lost by fire or other casualty; relief can be had only through statutory reimbursement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reimbursement only via act of March 3, 1885 (23 Stat. 350). Cases: P.63, 278 (Jan. 1894); C.10025 (Mar. 22, 1901); C.20143 (1906, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory issue conditioned on confinement term
rubrics_metrics.description: A statutory provision authorizing issuance of citizens' outer clothing to prisoners 'to be issued upon release from confinement... who has been confined under a court-martial sentence involving dishonorable discharge' does not apply where the sentence adjudged a dishonorable discharge without any term of confinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commutation rates set by regulation (not statute) but recognized by appropriations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority to establish rates of allowance for commutation of rations is not statutory but left to Army regulation; these amounts are recognized and sanctioned in Army appropriation acts relating to the Subsistence Department.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commutation for travel limited to travel period
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowance for commutation of rations payable to enlisted men traveling on detached duty when it is impracticable to carry rations is restricted to the period covered by the travel and not payable for rations consumed at the destination where the soldier is placed by orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: not payable for four days' board at destination hotel (P.59, 38, Apr. 1893).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential dismissal cannot deprive pay by implication
rubrics_metrics.description: A dismissal of an officer by order of the President does not involve deprivation of any part of the pay due him; an order expressed to dismiss 'without pay or allowances' is unauthorized and inoperative as to pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.10, 216 (Aug. 1864); other cases cited 1878–1880. Legal muster revocation cannot divest vested pay rights (e.g., R.42, 470, Jan. 19, 1880).

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive acts cannot date back to divest vested pay rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The Executive cannot make an order relate back so as to affect the status or rights of an officer or soldier as they existed before the taking effect of the dismissal; vested rights to pay cannot be nullified by retroactive dating-back of orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: R.6, 379, 405 (Sept./Oct. 1864); R.10, 1, 4 (July 1864); others through 1904.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension language should not be construed to forfeit pay by implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a sentence suspended an officer 'from the service for the term of six months,' in light of the principle that pay may not be forfeited by implication, such a sentence should be construed as suspension from rank/promotion/command only, not a forfeiture of pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.23, 427 (Apr. 1867). Avoid imputing broader forfeiture simply due to general phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 1766 R.S. and stoppages for arrears
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1766 (no money paid to persons in arrears until they account and pay) has not been strictly construed to preclude making stoppages against pay in monthly amounts that leave a margin for necessary living expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoppage example: $100 collected at $10 per month (C.7415, Dec. 1899; C.3292, Dec. 18, 1897). Accounting officers exercise discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowances beyond contract unauthorized
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer cannot authorize payment beyond the terms of a contract; allowances (e.g., travel expenses) in excess of contract stipulations are unauthorized and may be stopped against the paying officer's account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civilian assistant engaged at $150/month had travel expenses paid; those were unauthorized and legally stopped (P.43, 182, Oct. 1890).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay cannot be stopped for private company claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay due an officer or soldier cannot legally be stopped to reimburse a private company (e.g., telegraph company) for money received by a service member for private messages; indebtedness to a private company is not a debt to the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P.61, 185 (Aug. 1893); C.20083 (July 30, 1906). An officer/soldier cannot be mulcted of pay for satisfaction of a private claim (multiple cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoppage vs fine/forfeiture (nature and authorization)
rubrics_metrics.description: A stoppage is a charge on account (a means of reimbursement); a fine or forfeiture is punishment imposed for an offense. A stoppage cannot, absent statute or regulation, be imposed as punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P.36, 87 (Oct. 1889). But it is legal to stop pay to reimburse the United States for damage to public property while simultaneously bringing the soldier to court-martial (P.62, 481; C.18115).

rubrics_metrics.name: No stoppage to satisfy personal indebtedness to other service members absent sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States is not authorized to stop against pay amounts of personal indebtedness owed by an officer or soldier to another officer or soldier, unless there is a sentence of court-martial forfeiting the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims from erroneous final statements: private claim not collectible from United States
rubrics_metrics.description: If a discharged soldier's final statements call for more than was due and payment was made, the difference can be the subject of a claim against the discharged soldier (assignor) but not against the United States; stoppage against a reenlisted soldier to satisfy a private claim is not authorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoppage recommended for misappropriation of company funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Where officers misappropriate company funds, it is appropriate to recommend stopping the misappropriated amount against their pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stopping pay to reimburse company fund of deceased officer
rubrics_metrics.description: If an officer's estate shows a debt to a company fund and the Government owes him the same amount (e.g., unendorsed check payable to his order), the amount may be stopped against pay due the deceased officer and the check canceled/returned to drawer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture under Executive order limits forfeiture to pay due at date of discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Executive order (Mar. 30, 1898), a sentence that forfeits 'all pay and allowances' means forfeiture of pay and allowances due at the date of the discharge; a court-martial cannot award confinement and forfeiture greater than the prescribed limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.3694 (Apr. 1898) and other cited cases; order later amended (G.O.88, A.G.O., 1900) to address limits when dishonorable discharge not adjudged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of remission on forfeiture timing
rubrics_metrics.description: If a dishonorable discharge is remitted in approving the sentence, the forfeiture intended to relate to pay due at the date of discharge becomes applicable only to pay due at the date of receipt at the post of the order publishing the sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment before promulgation vests title to pay
rubrics_metrics.description: If pay is received by an officer or soldier before the promulgation or official notice of a forfeiture sentence, the payment vests and cannot be reclaimed from the recipient; the paymaster who paid was not accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.10, 609 (Nov. 1864); cases showing a soldier paid while confined had title unaffected by later forfeiture (e.g., a.3258, June 1897; C.14787, 1903; C.16955, 1904).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture affects only pay under pending contract
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence expressly forfeiting all pay due applies only to pay due under the pending enlistment/contract and will not affect pay due for service rendered under a previous enlistment that has not yet been settled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing rule: promulgation vs notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Army Regulations prescribe that confinement and forfeiture, when the sentence is silent as to timing, are operative from promulgation in orders (an exception to the general rule that orders affecting status or rights take effect from notice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, where specific regulation or context is absent, the general rule (effective from notice) applies — example of a cadet whose commuted suspension took effect from notice (P.64, 280, Apr. 1894).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture of 'pay due and to become due' includes commutation allowances
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence to forfeit 'pay due and to become due' forfeits commutation of quarters, fuel, and rations — these are included in 'allowances.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture period: necessary clothing and subsistence protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a sentence forfeits 'all pay and allowances' for a certain period, necessary clothing may still be supplied; all prisoners in manual custody are entitled to subsistence during detention, and subsistence cannot be forfeited by sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Destruction of trial record before review can operate as acquittal
rubrics_metrics.description: If the record of trial is destroyed before the reviewing authority acts and cannot be reproduced, the destruction has the legal effect of an acquittal and relieves the accused from forfeiture of pay due at date of the offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeited pay becomes public money in Treasury; restoration requires Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: Money forfeited by sentence and returning to the appropriation is public money in the Treasury and cannot be withdrawn and restored to the party except by authority of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.23, 642/659 (Aug. 1867); other cases and opinions (C.11594, Jan. 1903; C.14068, Jan. 1903; C.15510, Nov. 1903). Constitutional Article I, §9, §7 referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition of forfeitures for Volunteer Army
rubrics_metrics.description: Money accruing from forfeitures due to sentences in cases of Volunteer Army soldiers should be left in the Treasury and credited to the pay of the Army.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clothing money on discharge without honor (except fraudulent enlistment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier does not forfeit clothing money due him at the date of discharge if discharged without honor, except in cases of fraudulent enlistment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-martial findings not conclusive on civil liability; acquittal doesn't preclude contractual forfeiture
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial enforces military discipline and is not conclusive as to civil liability; an acquittal of desertion does not prevent forfeiture of pay and allowances accruing during absence as prescribed by regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.12168 (Mar. 6, 1902). Distinguish criminal acquittal from civil contractual obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent enlistment forfeits travel allowance entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who entered the Army by fraudulent enlistment is not entitled, upon summary discharge without honor, to travel allowance; the defrauded contracting party may rescind the contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P.54, 373 (July 1892). Act of rescission principle applied to enlistment contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge by reason of civil punishment forfeits travel pay (Sec.1290 R.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier discharged without honor from the Army because of punishment by a civil tribunal may be considered discharged 'by way of punishment for an offense' under section 1290 R.S., and therefore not entitled to travel pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharges by favor subject to waiver of travel allowances
rubrics_metrics.description: Discharges granted by way of favor are subject to a waiver of travel allowances; the soldier applying for such discharge consents to the waiver as a condition of being granted the discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.15176 (Sept. 4, 1903); C.1862 (Dec. 1895). Department commander cannot refuse to forward applications; discharge only by President or Secretary of War.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonorable discharge results in loss of travel pay by operation of law
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier sentenced to dishonorable discharge forfeits travel pay under section 1290 R.S. as a matter of operation of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of government property can be charged against pay when findings disapproved
rubrics_metrics.description: Where government property (e.g., revolver) was lost and the accused was acquitted but findings disapproved, the cost of the instrument may be charged against the soldier's pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only courts-martial can impose fines; fines accrue to United States
rubrics_metrics.description: The fine known to military law is that imposed by sentence of court-martial; no military commander may impose a fine, fines adjudged by courts-martial accrue to the United States and cannot be imposed for the benefit of an individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: B.8, 444 (May 1864); R.7, 52/643 (Jan./May 1864); R.8, 298 (Apr. 1864). A court-martial cannot direct collection by provost marshal—such directions are surplusage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fine (punishment) and stoppage (reimbursement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fine is punishment imposed by court-martial; a stoppage is an enforced reimbursement or 'charge on account' entered against pay for amounts due the United States or expressly authorized by law/regulation to be charged for amounts due an individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.35, 457 (July 1874); P.38, 88 (Jan. 1890). Use statutory/regulatory authorization for stoppages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remission of forfeiture limited to pay not yet due; illegal sentences refundable
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence forfeiting pay can be remitted only as to pay not due and payable at the date of the remission; if a sentence was illegal and void, the soldier should be credited on subsequent rolls and refunded the amount illegally collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple cases: R.1, 393 (Oct. 1862); R.8, 392/576 (June 1864); various Comptroller opinions and cases through 1904 (C.5392; C.11594; C.11742; C.11576; C.12596; C.16955).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commutation of dismissal to suspension does not forfeit pay
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sentence of dismissal (e.g., of a West Point cadet) is commuted to suspension, the suspension does not involve a forfeiture of pay.
